title: The rebbe
hook: a Hasidic leader seen as guide and channel for his followers

segments.voice: Yesterday, simcha, joy as the force that opens the heart. Your line was joy opens. Did you catch yourself clenching, and find one small good thing? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

A long table on a Friday night. At the head sits one man, and around him, packed shoulder to shoulder, some standing on benches, are his followers. He hardly speaks. He tastes a little of the food in front of him, and what's left is passed out into the crowd, and people reach for a crumb of it. Then someone starts a melody with no words, and the whole room picks it up. Hasidim call a gathering like this a tish, a table. The man at the head of it has a title of his own, and it's today's word.
screen: `A LONG TABLE ON A FRIDAY NIGHT.` → `A CRUMB PASSED INTO THE CROWD.` → `THE MAN AT THE HEAD.`

segments.voice: Rebbe. It's the Yiddish way of saying rabbi, and among Hasidim it means something particular: the leader of a Hasidic community, the one his followers turn to. First, the guide. Long before Hasidism, the Mishnah gives a piece of advice in Pirkei Avot: make for yourself a teacher. Not find one, make one, as if choosing a guide is something you do on purpose. Hasidim took that seriously. A follower brings the rebbe questions about prayer, but also about a marriage, a business, a sick child. Second, the channel. Hasidic teaching speaks of the tzaddik, the righteous one, and sees the rebbe this way: someone so attached to God that blessing flows through him to the people around him, and their prayers rise with his. That's why a crumb from his plate matters to them. Third, the bond goes both ways. A rebbe carries his followers in his heart and in his prayers, and the followers' devotion is part of how the community holds together. Fourth, and fairly: not every Jew sees it this way. Some Jewish communities, from early on, were wary of giving one person that much weight, and preferred to center life on study and the rabbi as a scholar and judge. Hasidim and their critics have argued it out, and both sides would say they are guarding something precious. Today we're simply meeting the rebbe as Hasidim do: a guide, and in Hasidic teaching, more than a guide.
screen: `MAKE FOR YOURSELF A TEACHER.` · `A CHANNEL FOR BLESSING.` · `THE BOND GOES BOTH WAYS.` · `NOT EVERY JEW SEES IT THIS WAY.` · then, large: `A GUIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a guide in your life. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who has helped you see your way. A teacher, a grandparent, a coach, a boss, a friend who told you the hard thing at the right time. Picture their face. Remember one sentence they said to you, or one thing they did that you still carry. Notice what it was that let you trust them. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. If they're still alive, you might decide to tell them. The bell holds the time.
Rebbe. The Yiddish form of rabbi, and for Hasidim the leader of a community: a guide, and in Hasidic teaching, a channel of blessing. Today's word.
Your line: a guide. Today, send one short message to someone who guided you, or tell someone else about them. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Hasidim visit their rebbe for blessing and advice, gather at his tish on Sabbaths and festivals to hear his teaching and sing, and often write to him with requests for prayer.
